record.original_question: If Δ is the maximum vertex degree of a nontrivial graph G, does there always exist a signature σ such that the spectral radius of the resulting signed graph satisfies ρ(G, σ) < 2 sqrt(Δ - 1)?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.25 ([46]). If ∆ is the largest vertex degree of a nontrivial graph G, then there exists a signature σ such that ρ(G, σ) < 2 √ ∆ − 1.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph with at least one edge, and let $\Delta=\Delta(G)$ denote the maximum degree of a vertex of $G$. A signature on $G$ is a function $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$; the pair $(G,\sigma)$ is called a signed graph. The signed adjacency matrix $A_\sigma=(a_{uv})$ is the symmetric $|V|\times|V|$ matrix with $a_{uv}=\sigma(uv)$ if $uv\in E$ and $a_{uv}=0$ otherwise. The spectral radius of the signed graph is
$$\rho(G,\sigma)=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }A_\sigma\}.$$
Prove or disprove: for every such graph $G$ there exists a signature $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ such that
$$\rho(G,\sigma)<2\sqrt{\Delta-1}.$$
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture (attributed to Gregory) appears in surveys of open problems in the spectral theory of signed graphs and is generalization of the Bilu–Linial conjecture (which concerns regular graphs and largest eigenvalue, partially addressed by Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava). No published resolution of the conjecture for general graphs with maximum degree $\Delta$ was located, so it appears to remain open as of 2026.
